chapter: Pay, the Fletcher Henderson circle and later life
title: Coltrane on soprano and the difficulty of the straight soprano
summary: Dance heard Coltrane's soprano as bagpipes; Caldwell and Hodges agree the straight soprano is hard to play.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Well, some of the sopranos -- I mean the first time I heard Coltrane playing the soprano, now, I know it was at Randall's Island, and, you know, the amplification was bad. It was outdoors in this big thing, Horace Silver I know but I went in there and (unintelligible) because he lives up in Connecticut. That's his home.
And But Horace was standing near the gate when I went in. I said, what is that sound? Is somebody playing the bagpipes? Sounded just like bagpipes, and he said, no, that's Coltrane playing soprano.
That was a horrible -- you know, I'd been brought up on Bechet and Johnny Hodges, and that was awful. I mean most of them, they have such a raucous sound.

Stanley, the truth is, That's -- like I was saying before (unintelligible) everybody can't develop a tone on that horn, and you got to have more of -- now, the (unintelligible) is type one beautiful, but that straight (unintelligible), and you can't do
what you want like you can play on another instrument like on another saxophone.
That's what Johnny Hodges told me.
You can't pick that up, he said.
You've got to work on it and lip up to play that.
